title: VB4-00693
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Mexico, seeks refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the "Act").1 The claimant's identity has been established through a certified copy of the claimant's passport and by her testimony.2 ALLEGATIONS

The claimant fears return to Mexico because she alleges that on XXXX XXXX, 2013, she and her husband were stopped at a checkpoint and five policemen wearing baklavas asked her husband for his identification. She further alleges that these policemen pulled her husband out of the car and began beating him. She alleges that these policemen approached her side of the car and she ran away. She alleges that the policemen shot at her, but they did not get her. She alleges that she took a cab to the bus terminal and took the bus to San Luis Colorado to a friend's home close to the United States (U.S.) border. She alleges that she left Mexico on XXXX XXXX, 2013 and arrived on foot in Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014. The claimant gave birth to her baby girl on XXXX XXXX, 2014 in British Colombia. The claimant made a refugee claim in February 2014.

The panel finds that the claimant has not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, or that on a balance of probabilities she faces a personal risk to her life or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if she returns to Mexico. Therefore, the panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee pursuant to section 96 of the Act nor a person in need of protection pursuant to section 97(1) of the Act for the reasons that follow. ANALYSIS Credibility and Nexus s.96 Convention Refugee

Credibility is the determinative issue in this case. The panel has considered in the Chairperson's Gender Guideline Four in making its decision. The claimant is a young 19-year old woman who gave birth to her first baby on XXXX XXXX, 2014 in Canada. Her baby is approximately one month at the time of the hearing. The claimant was provided breaks when needed to care for her baby and the panel has considered the claimant's circumstances in assessing the claimant's credibility.

Although the panel notes that the claimant testified that she was nervous and her counsel submitted that the inconsistencies were minor in some cases and not related to the central elements of her claim in some cases, the panel finds that the cumulative effect of the inconsistencies undermines the claimant's credibility and nervousness, youth and a pregnancy are not sufficient to explain why the claimant did not testify in a consistent manner. Further, the panel notes that the claimant did not appear nervous and the panel made efforts to ensure that the claimant was comfortable and in a safe environment. The panel is not undertaking a microscopic examination or looking for a minutia of details, but expects that the claimant would be able to testify in a consistent manner with some detail regarding allegations she claims to have personal knowledge of. Although claimant's counsel submitted that people forget things and people's memories work differently, the panel does not have evidence before it indicating that the claimant has a medical condition resulting in memory loss or inability to provide greater details when asked to do so about incidents she alleges she was physically present at.

Minister's Counsel intervened on credibility given that the Biometric Data Report indicates that the claimant encountered U.S. immigration officials in San Luis, Arizona, U.S.A. on XXXX XXXX, 2013 and was returned to Mexico the next day and the claimant stated on her Canadian immigration forms that she has never been refused admission or ordered to leave any country and did not disclose her travel history outside of Mexico prior to leaving Mexico in XXXX 2013.3

Claimant's Counsel submitted that the Minister's Intervention on credibility regarding the Claimant's misrepresentations regarding her failure to disclose her previous travel to the United States in XXXX 2013 do not seriously undermine the Claimant's refugee claim as this misrepresentation has nothing to do with why she fled Mexico in XXXX 2013. Although the panel agrees with Claimant's Counsel regarding the point that this one misrepresentation does not necessarily undermine the presumption of truth, the panel finds that it does reflect the Claimant's willingness to misrepresent to Canadian Immigration authorities in the past and raises the issue of credibility. Further, the panel finds that it is not merely one inconsistency, which undermines the claimant's credibility, but rather the cumulative effect of inconsistencies in this case, which does so.

The claimant submitted a statutory declaration explaining that she did not disclose her previous travel to the U.S. to her lawyer or the immigration authorities because she did not think it was important to her claim, she was ashamed and her previous travel to the U.S. did not have anything to do with her reasons for her refugee claim.4

When the panel asked the claimant to explain why she had misrepresented her travel history to the U.S. to Canadian immigration authorities, she testified that she did not think it was important, she was embarrassed and she was sorry. When the claimant was asked when she traveled to the U.S. and why she travelled to the U.S., she testified that she traveled only once in XXXX 2013 because she thought she could make some money by XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

When the claimant was asked when she applied for her passport, she testified in XXXX, or XXXX, no she thought it was XXXX. When the claimant was asked to explain how this is possible given that her passport was issued on XXXX XXXX, 2013, she testified that she did not know the date. When the claimant was asked when she became aware that she was pregnant, she testified in XXXX 2013. When the claimant was asked why she applied for a passport in XXXX 2013, she testified that she wanted to get a visa to go to the U.S. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, but she never applied for a visa because she did not have the money to proceed with the application. When she was asked why she did not have her passport on her when she traveled to the U.S. in XXXX 2013, given that she had testified that she always kept her passport in her bag, she testified that she just didn't have it on her, she didn't have her bag or money with her. She testified that she had her bag with her the second time she left Mexico and that is why she had her passport on her person the second time she traveled.

The panel does not find the claimant's explanation for why she testified that she applied for her passport in September when it was issued in August or her reason for applying for the passport to buy clothes in the U.S. satisfactory. It is reasonable to expect that the claimant would know when approximately she applied for her passport given that she made the application herself. Further, it would be reasonable to expect that the claimant would have some money on her person if her purpose for her travel to the U.S. in XXXX 2013 was XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX contrary to her testimony that she did not have her bag or money with her in XXXX 2013. The panel finds that these inconsistencies undermine her credibility and are important because they undermine her allegation that it was out of fear that she fled Mexico the second time and she had unrelated reasons to leave Mexico in XXXX 2013.

When the claimant was asked why she left Mexico the second time, she testified that people are kidnapped and there is no ransom demanded. When the claimant was asked why she personally left Mexico, she testified that she and her husband were stopped by the police, they asked her husband for ID, he gave it to them and before he was out of the car, they pushed him and started beating him up. She testified that two of them approached her side of the door, she ran and they shot at her, but fortunately she was not hit. When she was asked how many men there were, she testified that she did not know for sure, it was dark, but four or five men. She testified that she knew they were policemen by the way they were dressed and by their police vehicles. When she was asked if she could provide any further details about the incident she testified that she could not. The panel finds that the claimant's vagueness undermines her credibility as it would be reasonably expected that she could provide more details regarding what happened, what she saw, heard and experienced on the alleged XXXX XXXX, 2013 incident with the police, which is central to her claim.

When the claimant was asked if she or anyone in her family had any interactions with police officers prior to XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013, she testified, "No." When the claimant was asked directly if her husband had any interactions with police officers before XXXX XXXX, 2013, she testified, "No." When the claimant was asked to explain why in her Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative she alleges that two police officers came to her home on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013 and spoke to her husband for about 10 to 15 minutes, she testified that she did not know why she did not remember this event in her testimony. The panel does not find this explanation satisfactory and undermines her credibility as it is reasonable to expect that the claimant would remember the only two times she saw her husband encounter the police in Mexico, given that her fear of the police in Mexico is central to her claim.

When the claimant was asked if anyone chased her when she ran away from the policemen, she testified that she did not look back. Given the proximity of the claimant's description of events, that two men approached her side of the vehicle and she ran away, the claimant was asked how she thought she was able to get away. She testified that she did not know; it was a miracle. The panel finds that given the credibility issues already noted, as well as the allegations that two police officers approached her door and she ran away and was able to run for 10 to 15 minutes to the nearby supermarket without these men catching her, the panel finds on a balance of probabilities, it is unlikely that two armed police officers would not have been able to catch a young woman who was approximately six months pregnant if they were seriously interested in pursuing her. As a result, the panel finds that the claimant's allegation that the police were after her is not supported by sufficient credible evidence.

The claimant testified that her husband did not have any criminal charges against him and that as far as she knew he was not involved in the drug trade. She also submitted evidence regarding an acquaintance of her husband, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and is rumored to have links with drug dealers, but he denies the allegations.5 She also submitted a letter from a friend of her husband who indicates that the claimant's husband was friends with XXXX XXXX as he would see them together at his upholstery shop and eating tacos together on the street.6 The article regarding XXXX XXXX does not corroborate the kidnapping of the claimant's husband or any association between the claimant's husband and XXXX XXXX. The letter from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX indicates that he has not seen the claimant's husband in three or four months and people are saying he is missing and was kidnapped.7 The panel gives little weight to this letter as it is speculative regarding what has happened to the claimant's husband and relies on hearsay.

The claimant testified that neither she nor her brother nor her mother had any interactions with police officers prior to XXXX XXXX, 2013. She testified that she has never committed any criminal offences; there are no charges against her and no warrant for her arrest. She testified that she told her mother not to make a police report or get involved because it is dangerous. The claimant testified that she has never been involved in the drug trade in Mexico. When the claimant was asked why she thought the authorities would be interested in her, she testified that she did not know.

When the claimant was asked why she had not included in her BOC the fact that men were coming to her mother's home looking for her, she testified that she did not know this when she provided her narrative in XXXX 2014 and it was only subsequent to this that she learned these men were looking for her at her home. When the claimant was asked why she did not include this amendment when she submitted her statutory declaration subsequent to Minister's Intervention on XXXX XXXX, 2014, she testified that before she received her mother's letter she had spoken to her mother and knew that these men had come looking for her once, but she was surprised to see that her mother had written, "several times." She testified that she was in the hospital when the documents from Mexico arrived at her address in Canada and her landlord took these documents for her to her lawyer. Claimant's Counsel submitted that she did not think to ask her client to amend the narrative with this new information as the mother's letter had already been submitted and the claimant's credibility should not be undermined by this failure to update the BOC prior to the hearing.

The claimant testified that she has not spoken to her mother in two weeks. The claimant testified that she asked her mother for a letter in XXXX, it was received by her landlord who then took the letter to her lawyer. The claimant testified that she has tried to make calls to her mother's cell phone, but has not been able to get through and has not been able to leave messages for her mother. The claimant testified that her two brothers, ages 21 and 13 also live in XXXX XXXX. She testified that her 13-year old brother lives with their mother, but does not have a cell phone. She testified that her 21-year old brother lives in a different neighborhood in XXXX XXXX; he keeps changing his phone number and she is not able to reach him either. She testified that she has other relatives, but they live on farms far away without a signal and she cannot contact them either to find out why she is unable to reach her mother by phone.

Although the panel accepts that the claimant and her counsel did not update the BOC given that the mother's letter had already been submitted, the panel gives the mother's letter little weight. The mother's letter is undated, vague, lacking in details or description regarding when, where, and who has come several times for her daughter, which is information the mother would be reasonably expected to provide if she has firsthand information regarding corrupt authorities' or criminals' interest in her daughter.8 The claimant's mother's letter provides some details regarding the abduction of her son-in-law, but given that the claimant's mother was not there on XXXX XXXX XXXX2014, she would only have secondhand information regarding this event. Accordingly, the panel finds that the claimant has not provided sufficient reliable evidence that the police in Mexico are looking for her based on her mother's letter and who cannot be reached by phone.

The panel finds that the claimant's fears of return to Mexico are not a result of her gender or imputed political opinion. The panel finds that the claimant's fears involve a young woman whose husband may or may not have been involved in drug trafficking or associated with others who may be involved with drug trafficking who may have been abducted by either criminals posing as police officers or corrupt police officers or he was arrested by police officers using excessive means to detain him.

Claimant's counsel submitted that the claimant has established a nexus given that she fears the authorities who she alleges engaged in the enforced disappearance of her husband on XXXX XXXX, 2013 and the documentary evidence indicates that there is collusion between narco-traffickers and the authorities in Mexico in enforced disappearances.9 The panel finds that the claimant has not established that she has a link to an imputed political opinion. The claimant has not provided evidence that she has made any public complaints about the widespread corrupt conduct of government officials against XXXX XXXX or any corrupt police officers in Mexico or that she would be perceived as having a political opinion against corrupt state agents in Mexico. When the claimant was asked if she or her mother has made any complaints against the alleged four or five corrupt police officers who she believes beat and abducted her husband, she testified that they had not done so. Although the claimant alleges that she fears corrupt police officers who she alleges engaged in criminal conduct, namely abducting her husband, she has not established that she is perceived as opposing the state of Mexico because of her views against the widespread corruption among the police force.

The panel recognizes that in some cases, such as Klinko v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [2000] 3. F.C. 327 (C.A.), a claimant may establish nexus as political opinion. Klinko, supra involved a case where a man made a complaint regarding the widespread corruption in the Ukraine, suffered retaliation as a result and was therefore perceived as taking a position against the state. The facts of the case at hand are distinguished from Klinko, supra as the claimant has not established that she has denounced or has made any public complaints regarding unsanctioned corruption in Mexico and would therefore be persecuted because she is perceived to have a political opinion against the state.

In consideration of the Chairperson's Gender Guideline Four,10 the panel has considered that the claimant may have limited information regarding her husband's associations and work activities given the socio-cultural context of a young 19-year old woman from Mexico who is married to a 40 year old man who did not share much about his work or associations with her. The claimant made no allegations of abuse by her husband in her BOC or in her testimony, nor did her counsel make any submissions regarding gender-related persecution she would face if she returns to Mexico. Although the panel appreciates that the claimant may not have much information regarding the reasons why her husband may have been abducted, she has not established that she would be perceived as opposing the state because of an abduction of her husband by corrupt police officers. Although claimant's counsel submitted significant documentary evidence regarding enforced disappearances in Mexico,11 which is consistent with the Immigration and Refugee Board's (the "Board") documentary evidence, the onus is on the claimant to link her circumstances to the documentary evidence and the panel finds that she has not done so. Accordingly, based on the totality of the evidence the panel finds that the claimant has not established a nexus and has not satisfied the burden that she would face more than a mere possibility of persecution if she returns to Mexico. Section 97(1)Person in Need of Protection

For the reasons highlighted above, the panel finds that the claimant has not provided sufficient reliable credible evidence to establish on a balance of probabilities that she faces a personal risk to her life or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if she returns to Mexico.

For the foregoing reasons, the panel determines that the claimant is not a Convention refugee under section 96 of the Act or a person in need of protection under section 97(1) of the Act. The Board therefore rejects her claim.
